Skip next section Officials: 'attempted attack' on power grid outside of Berlin 09/01/2026 September 1, 2026 Officials: 'attempted attack' on power grid outside of Berlin The Jänschwalde plant generates electricity by burning coal Image: Patrick Pleul/dpa/picture alliance German authorities have released more details about a suspected attack on an electric power station in the eastern German state of Brandenburg. Police found several homemade explosive devices near the electrical substation in Turnow-Preilack, southeast of Berlin. Local network operator 50Hertz described the devices as small rockets resembling New Year’s Eve fireworks. Some of the devices had been launched while others were found unexploded, the operator said. There was a brief power cut, but all power ‌lines are back in operation The Turnow-Preilack substation is where the electricity from the Jänschwalde power plant is distributed across the region. Brandenburg State Premier Dietmar Woidke called it an "attempted attack" and condemned the act. "The worryingly high frequency of such incidents shows that we must decisively protect our infrastructure," he said. The suspected sabotage follows a series of recent strikes on the power grid around Berlin. In January, an arson attack by suspected far-left extremists on power lines in left 45,000 households in the German capital without electricity for days. In March 2024, another group targeted an electricity pylon, cutting power to a Tesla factory outside of Berlin. https://p.dw.com/p/5K1WH Skip next section Germany's Antonio Rüdiger retires from international football 09/01/2026 September 1, 2026 Germany's Antonio Rüdiger retires from international football Rüdiger said he felt the time had come to pass the torch to the younger generation Image: Markus Ulmer/Pressefoto Ulmer/picture alliance German central defender Antonio Rüdiger has announced his retirement from international football, saying he wanted to "clear the path for the younger generation" after the 2026 World Cup exit. Last month, a court in Hamburg sentenced seven young members of the terror group to prison terms ranging from one and a half to five years. https://p.dw.com/p/5Jw4W Skip next section Merz: No coalition, but some kind of interplay with Left Party possible in Saxony-Anhalt 09/01/2026 September 1, 2026 Merz: No coalition, but some kind of interplay with Left Party possible in Saxony-Anhalt Chancellor Friedrich Merz has expanded on how he hopes a CDU-led coalition — presumably without a clear majority — could still govern in Saxony-Anhalt after Sunday's elections . Polls suggest the right-wing populist Alternative for Germany (AfD) will be by far the largest party , with the CDU a distant second, and the socialist Left Party ( die Linke ) next in line. Given that the CDU refuses to join a coalition or formally "work together" with either the AfD on the right or the Left Party, this could make establishing a functioning government extremely challenging. "With both the AfD and the Left there are such fundamental differences to the [Christian Democratic] Union, that direct cooperation is out of the question," Merz told the local Mitteldeutsche Zeitung and Magdeburger Volksstimme newspapers on Tuesday. But Merz said that some kind of CDU-led minority government operating with support from individuals in the Left Party on a policy-by-policy basis had proven viable in other states. "We see how it's possible to govern in Thuringia and Saxony ," he said of two other eastern states where the AfD is either the strongest single party, or a close and influential second. "But it needs to be clear that there are limits," Merz added, saying he felt these limits lay in holding Cabinet positions and formulating government policy. Can this also work in Saxony-Anhalt? Numerically, the parliamentary arithmetic could be more problematic in Saxony-Anhalt than any other state to date, at least based on the opinion polls prior to Sunday's vote. In Thuringia the CDU-led government only needs to convince one opposition politician of a policy to command a majority. In Saxony, that figure rises to 10 but there are more oppositon parties to try to woo. Depending on Sunday's results, it's conceivable that a CDU-led minority government without the AfD or the Left Party could command fewer than 40% of the seats, or fewer still if the Greens fail to clear the 5% hurdle and enter parliament. And it would likely only have one party, the Left, to try to win over, assuming it planned to continue to exclude the AfD. Prior to the vote, the Left in Saxony-Anhalt have said their condition would be having a more direct say on policy plans. How both sides might define this, and what compromises they might be willing to entertain once the results are in on Sunday night, remains unclear for now. https://p.dw.com/p/5JuaO Skip next section Explosive devices discovered at substation in eastern Germany 09/01/2026 September 1, 2026 Explosive devices discovered at substation in eastern Germany The Jänschwalde coal-fired power plant was built between 1976 and 1989 Image: Andreas Franke/IMAGO Police have found several explosive devices near the Jänschwalde power station in the eastern German state of Brandenburg, according to media reports on Tuesday. The number of part-time workers increased 0.5% compared to the same period last year, to 16.936 million. At the same time, the number of full-time workers fell by 0.9% to 25.138 million. The IAB named two reasons for the trend. It said there had been employment growth in sectors with a high proportion of part-time work , such as health care and teaching. It also cited job cuts in sectors dominated by full-time work, such as manufacturing. "The economy has recently stabilized, so the working hours of employees are rising slightly again," said the IAB's Enzo Weber. "But the crisis-hit manufacturing sector is losing many full-time jobs, meaning that overall fewer hours were worked." The average weekly working hours for full-time employees remained constant at 38.32 hours in the second quarter. For part-time workers, it rose slightly to 18.88 hours. She added that the company was required to honor commitments made to workers under an agreement reached in 2024. Around 30,000 jobs depend on the Emden plant in northern Germany, Benner said, while the Zwickau site is particularly important for eastern Germany. She argued there was "plenty of time to develop prospects for both sites" and said announcements about further potential cost-cutting measures had only created confusion and undermined morale among workers.
